raw_case_text:
During a routine checkup in 2005, a 43-year-old man was diagnosed with polycythemia vera with the JAK2 mutation. Serum erythropoietin (Epo) level was low, which corresponded to the diagnosis of polycythemia vera. The patient rejected treatment because he had no symptoms. A year later, he reported abdominal pain and an investigation indicated portal and splenic vein thrombosis. He was started on 1500-2000 mg/dl hydroxycarbamide, acetylsalicylic acid, and oral anticoagulant medication, with regular INR checks and phlebotomies. A medical examination in 2011 found that the thrombotic veins had not been recanalized, the spleen was 230 mm, the accessory spleen was 50 mm, and grade I/II varicosities were present in the distal esophagus and proximal stomach.
The patient was taken to the hospital in October 2018 with a fever and headache. Standard tests were performed, which revealed that the repeated blood culture, urine culture, and the patient's HIV status were negative. IgM antibodies to the West Nile virus (WNV) were found in the serum, and C. neoformans was found in the cerebrospinal fluid culture. It is known that disseminated cryptococcosis can occur in immunocompromised patients.   We suspected this because in that period there was an epidemic of WNV infection in Europe and Serbia, which can be asymptomatic.
A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed that seven heterogeneous and inhomogeneous hyperintense T2 lesions up to 10 x 14 mm in diameter are observed in the head of the caudate nucleus bilaterally more pronounced on the right (Figure 1(a)), in the genu of the internal capsule, and the globus pallidus on the left (Figure 1(a)) without diffusion restriction (Figure 1(d)-(g)) and post-contrast enhancement of the signal intensity (Figure 1 (h) and (i)). Similar but less oval, inhomogeneous lesions can be seen along the body of the left lateral ventricle parietal (Figure 1(b)), in the center of the semioval on the right, as well as frontally and parietal on the left in the center of the semioval (Figure 1(c)). The described lesions correspond to dilated perivascular spaces in the sense of gelatinous pseudocysts, which are typical for C. neoformans but are not seen in WNV infection. In Cryptococcus infection, lesions can also occur in the basal nuclei and changes are more homogeneous and diffuse. Thus, in the case of cryptococcal infection, the presence of pseudocysts has been reported as a specific finding on MRI. The post-contrast FLAIR sequence shows dural augmentation of signal intensity occipitoparietal more pronounced left, as well as the gyral-leptomeningeal frontoparietal bilateral more prominent right (Figure 2). Dural and leptomeningeal enhancement of signal intensity can characterize both C. neoformans and WNV infections and cannot be denied neuroradiologically because they occur in both entities.
Antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day i.v.) and fluconazole (initial dose 2 x 400 mg p.o. first day, followed with 1 x 400 mg p.o.) was started. After 3 months of the treatment, the fever and headache decreased, and the cerebrospinal fluid culture remained negative after 2 weeks of incubation. Antifungal therapy was stopped, but the patient rapidly acquired a fever of 39 C, increased leukocyte count to 46 x 109/l (Table 1), and became bradypsychic and bradykinetic. On January 23, 2019, an abdomen computed tomography scan was performed. The findings revealed a 206 mm liver, mildly dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, a 277 x 222 x 105 mm spleen, a cavernous portal vein, a thrombosed splenic vein, and an auxiliary spleen of prior size. The oral anticoagulant, hydroxycarbamide, and fluconazole medication were continued for an additional 9 months. After the blood test results reverted to normal, hydroxycarbamide was ruled out. The patient developed cardiac insufficiency with pro-BNP levels of 12.000 ng/l. CD4+ cells were 150/mm3 (Table 1) at the time, and CD8 lymphocytes were 243/mm3. Even without hydroxycarbamide, hemoglobin was 100 g/l after 3 months of hospital therapy, white blood cells were 16 x 109/l, and platelets were 374 x 109/l, while bradypsychia and bradykinesia gradually disappeared. By the end of March 2019, polycythemia had worsened, and the liver and spleen were significantly enlarged. Because bone marrow cytology and biopsy revealed that polycythemia vera had progressed to post-polycythemic myelofibrosis, ruxolitinib (2 x 20 mg/day) was introduced on September 12th, 2019, along with prophylactic treatment with fluconazole 200 mg/d for the next 3 months. The liver and spleen were greatly reduced in size. Unfortunately, after 21 months of ruxolitinib treatment, he was diagnosed with epiglottic planocellular carcinoma, which required a laryngectomy and radiotherapy on August 16, 2019. The patient is currently stable on ruxolitinib, acetylsalicylic acid, and an oral anticoagulant therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old man with JAK2-positive polycythemia vera presented with fever and headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, diagnosed with JAK2-positive polycythemia vera in 2005 and portal/splenic vein thrombosis in 2006 managed with hydroxycarbamide, aspirin, oral anticoagulants, and phlebotomies, presented to the hospital in October 2018 with acute fever and headache during a regional West Nile virus epidemic.
subjective.past_medical_history: JAK2-positive polycythemia vera (diagnosed in 2005), portal and splenic vein thrombosis (2006), splenomegaly (230 mm) with accessory spleen (50 mm), and grade I/II gastroesophageal varices (2011).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and headache. Home medications included hydroxycarbamide (1500-2000 mg/day), acetylsalicylic acid, and oral anticoagulant medication.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with fever and headache; later developed fever of 39 C, bradypsychia, and bradykinesia after premature cessation of antifungals.
objective.routine_investigations: Repeated blood and urine cultures and HIV testing were negative. Serum West Nile virus (WNV) IgM antibodies were positive. During subsequent relapse/progression, WBC rose to 46 x 10^9/L, pro-BNP reached 12,000 ng/L, and 3 months later hemoglobin was 100 g/L, WBC 16 x 10^9/L, and platelets 374 x 10^9/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI revealed 7 heterogeneous T2-hyperintense lesions (up to 10 x 14 mm, consistent with gelatinous pseudocysts) in the bilateral caudate heads, left internal capsule genu, left globus pallidus, periventricular parietal region, and bilateral centrum semiovale without diffusion restriction or parenchymal enhancement, accompanied by bilateral frontoparietal leptomeningeal and left occipitoparietal dural FLAIR contrast enhancement. CSF culture grew Cryptococcus neoformans. Later evaluation showed CD4+ count 150/mm3 and CD8+ count 243/mm3, abdominal CT showing hepatosplenomegaly (liver 206 mm, spleen 277 x 222 x 105 mm) with cavernous portal vein and thrombosed splenic vein, and bone marrow biopsy confirming progression to post-polycythemic myelofibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis with basal ganglia gelatinous pseudocysts co-occurring with West Nile virus IgM positivity in a patient with polycythemia vera progressing to post-polycythemic myelofibrosis, confirmed by positive CSF culture for C. neoformans and characteristic brain MRI findings. Treated with IV liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day) and oral fluconazole (800 mg loading day 1, then 400 mg/day) for 3 months until CSF sterilization; rapid clinical relapse after stopping therapy required an additional 9 months of fluconazole and discontinuation of hydroxycarbamide. Subsequent progression to myelofibrosis was treated with ruxolitinib (20 mg twice daily) plus 3 months of fluconazole prophylaxis (200 mg/day); he later underwent laryngectomy and radiotherapy for epiglottic squamous cell carcinoma and remains stable.
